item.title: Detroit Lions to wear alternate uniforms in each of next 2 games
item.description: The Detroit Lions will wear two different alternate uniforms for their next two games.
item.content:encoded:
On Friday night, the Detroit Lions’ social media dropped a not-so-subtle hint about their next uniform combination. On Twitter, the Lions not only tweeted out a photo of a black Lions logo with a bright blue outline, but they also changed their Twitter logo to the same image.

Detroit has done this several times in the past, and it means only one thing: the black uniforms are coming out this upcoming week.

If you’re unfamiliar, the black Lions uniforms—dropped in 2024 and officially called Motor City Muscle—feature a black jersey, black pants, and a popping blue helmet with the black Lions logo. You can see it used in action below.

Assuming all the hint dropping is true, the Lions will wear these for their home Week 7 game against the Green Bay Packers next week.

The following week, the Lions host the Minnesota Vikings, and they’ve already announced that they will be wearing their new Rivalry Uniforms for that Week 8 divisional matchup. This offseason, the NFL announced and debuted the Rivalry design for all of the NFC North and AFC South teams. The Lions’ uniforms feature an all-grey look with black and blue stripes on the shoulder pads designed to mimic the eyes of a Lion. In Detroit’s debut photoshoot of the Rivalry uniforms, the jerseys and pants were paired with the same blue helmet from the Motor City Muscle uniforms.

So we’ve got a couple of weeks of non-traditional Lions uniforms for what will be a pivotal two-game stretch of divisional games out of Detroit’s Week 6 bye.

item.title: Chicago Bears Week 6 Flashbacks: A meltdown, a milestone, and a breakout
item.description: Hop aboard the Gridiron Time Machine with @iamcogs and take a trip down Week 6 Bears memory lane!
item.content:encoded:
1. 2006, Bears @ Cardinals: They Are Who We Thought They Were!

October 16, 2006 | Bears win 24-23

There are weird wins, and then there is what happened in Arizona on Monday Night Football in 2006.

The Bears entered Week 6 undefeated at 5-0 and looking like one of the best teams in football. By halftime, none of that seemed to matter. Arizona had built a 20-0 lead while Rex Grossman and the Chicago offense completely unraveled.

Grossman eventually finished just 14-of-37 for 144 yards, four interceptions and two lost fumbles. The Bears offense never scored a touchdown.

Somehow, Chicago still won.

The comeback began when Mark Anderson stripped Matt Leinart and Mike Brown recovered the fumble for a touchdown. Later, Brian Urlacher ripped the football away from Edgerrin James, allowing Charles Tillman to scoop it up and race 40 yards for another defensive score.

That still left the Bears trailing 23-17 with under three minutes remaining.

Enter Devin Hester.

Hester fielded a punt at his own 17-yard line, found daylight and took it 83 yards for the go-ahead touchdown, completing one of the most ridiculous comebacks in franchise history.

Arizona still had a chance to win, but Neil Rackers missed a 40-yard field goal in the closing seconds, allowing Chicago to escape with a 24-23 victory.

The numbers make the result even harder to believe. The Bears committed six turnovers, gained only 168 yards and did not score an offensive touchdown. Urlacher finished with 19 tackles and forced the fumble that completely changed the game.

Of course, the night became even more memorable after Cardinals coach Dennis Green stepped to the podium and delivered one of the most famous postgame rants in NFL history.

“They are who we thought they were!”

He wasn’t wrong.

The Bears were 6-0.

2. 2014, Bears @ Falcons: Cutler leads Chicago to its 750th victory

October 12, 2014 | Bears win 27-13

The Bears entered Week 6 desperately needing to get things moving in the right direction.

Back-to-back losses had dropped Chicago to 2-3, and a road trip to Atlanta presented another difficult challenge against Matt Ryan and a dangerous Falcons offense.

Instead, Jay Cutler put together one of his best performances in a Bears uniform.

Cutler completed 26-of-38 passes for 381 yards, one touchdown and no interceptions, setting what would stand as his highest single-game passing total during his time in Chicago.

He had plenty of help from his receivers.

Alshon Jeffery caught five passes for 136 yards, while Brandon Marshall added six receptions for 113. Matt Forte once again did a little bit of everything, finishing with 80 rushing yards, 77 receiving yards and two touchdowns.

Chicago led 13-3 at halftime, but Atlanta erased that advantage with 10 unanswered points in the third quarter.

With the game tied at 13, Cutler delivered the play that swung momentum back toward the Bears.

Facing third-and-long, he launched a deep ball down the sideline to Jeffery, who hauled it in for a 74-yard gain. Forte scored a touchdown shortly afterward, and Chicago never trailed again.

The Bears defense shut Atlanta out in the fourth quarter, while Forte added another touchdown to finish off a 27-13 victory.

Cutler’s performance and the win itself were already noteworthy, but the afternoon also carried some franchise history.

The victory was the 750th regular-season win in Chicago Bears history, making them the first NFL franchise to reach that mark.

A big road win, Cutler throwing for nearly 400 yards, and another number added to one of the league’s oldest franchises.

Not a bad afternoon in Atlanta.

3. 2024, Bears vs. Jaguars: Caleb Williams shines in London

October 13, 2024 | Bears win 35-16

The Bears traveled across the Atlantic in Week 6 of Caleb Williams’ rookie season with some momentum beginning to build.

By the time they left London, that momentum had turned into one of Williams’ first real statement performances as an NFL quarterback.

Jacksonville actually struck first and held a 3-0 lead after the opening quarter, but Chicago quickly took control.

Williams found Cole Kmet for a 31-yard touchdown early in the second quarter before connecting with him again from two yards out just before halftime. The Bears went into the locker room leading 14-3 and never really looked back.

Williams continued spreading the football around after halftime, this time finding Keenan Allen for a pair of touchdowns as Chicago’s lead continued to grow.

He finished the afternoon 23-of-29 for 226 yards, four touchdowns and one interception, while also causing problems with his legs by rushing for another 56 yards.

It was the first four-touchdown passing game of Williams’ young career.

Kmet caught five passes for 70 yards and two touchdowns, Allen added two scores of his own, and D’Andre Swift rushed for 91 yards and another touchdown as Chicago rolled to a 35-16 victory.

Kmet’s afternoon deserves a little extra appreciation as well.

When long snapper Scott Daly suffered a knee injury, Kmet suddenly found himself pulling double duty. Not only did he lead the Bears in receiving and catch two touchdowns, he also stepped in as Chicago’s emergency long snapper.

Because apparently catching touchdowns in London wasn’t enough.

The win moved Chicago to 4-2 and gave the Bears their third straight victory, while Williams walked away with the first four-touchdown game of hit young career.

For Bears fans watching from back home, waking up early turned out to be worth it.

Gary Baugher Jr. is a second year contributor to WCG, bringing football insight backed by over 16 years of experience in organized football and more than 30 years as a passionate fan of the game. You can follow him on Twitter at @iamcogs.

item.title: Big Blue View mailbag: Cam Skattebo, ‘peanut punch’, more questions
item.description: The mail’s here! Questions, answers about your first-place Giants.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Stolzenberger asks: A lot has been made, rightfully, about the Commanders’ poor deciding and executing at the end of OT in game 5. But wouldn’t it have been much safer and smarter for the Giants to have tried the field goal on 2nd down (I think it was) instead of handing it off to Skattebo for a couple of more yards up the middle? They were already inside the 25 yard line and any score would have won the game immediately. Winston had been on fire and the Washington defense was pretty grabby already on every play. Seems to me I recall Parcells and other team’s coaches not waiting for 4th down or taking more time off the clock in similar situations — rather just get it over with. Also, who would make that call, the OC or Harbaugh? We should be 4-1.

Ed says: Robert, no. Stay with me, and I will explain.

Skattebo ran for 5 yards and a first down right before the overtime two-minute warning. So, what you are asking is if the Giants should have simply kicked the field goal on first down coming out of the two-minute warning. Now, of course if the Giants make the kick there they win the game, Both teams had already possessed the ball once.

But … there is always a’but’.

Remember that placekicker Dominic Zvada missed three of five field-goal tries in the game, and had already missed from 46 yards during overtime. Washington had already used its two allotted timeouts in overtime.

Yes, if you make the kick there you win the game. If you miss, though, you are handing the ball to Washington at about the 32-yard line with 1:50 to play. They have plenty of time to go down the field and kick a game-winning field goal, even without timeouts. We saw that play out. Had the Commanders not screwed up the clock management they moved down the field after the fumble and had plenty of time to get off a makeable field-goal try.

The idea is to run the ball twice, maybe three times and work the clock down so that the game-winning field goal try by Zvada would be the final play of the game. That way, you take away any chance Washington has of winning the game.

Here is how Harbaugh explained it Sunday night:

“The idea was to run it twice, and then run it down, get as close as we could, protect the football, which we talked about numerous times, and then run it down and take the knee. So in case he doesn’t make the field goal, there’s no time for them to come back and get the field goal. That’s the strategy.”

It was absolutely the proper way to play the situation. If Skattebo does his job, the Giants leave the Commanders with no opportunity to win. The only other way to do it is to take a knee three straight times, but that does result in moving the ball back a bit.

Peter Calamari asks: I wonder jf anyone says a connection between the deterioration of the Giants running game and the substitution of Hudson for Schmitz at center. It seems like since that switch was made the Giants are running much less effectively although possibly pass blocking somewhat better.

Ed says: Peter, it’s not the move to Bryan Hudson at center in place of John Michael Schmitz. Hudson has been better than Schmitz. If you judge by Pro Football Focus grades, which isn’t always the best way to judge, Hudson has been about 30 points better as both a run- and pass-blocker.

The difference is adjusting to a run game where the big difference-maker was supposed to be Jaxson Dart’s mobility. Dart’s Week 1 22-yard run is still the longest of the season for the Giants. Without the threat of the quarterback run game, the Giants are much more predictable and limited on the ground. Neither Cam Skattebo nor Najee Harris are guys who can outrun NFL defenders or possess enough wiggle to make defenders miss.

The blocking has to be perfect, and with teams loading up the box and outnumbering the Giants at the line of scrimmage it hasn’t been.

Another thing that doesn’t help is Andrew Thomas’s groin injury. He is clearly laboring to get through games, and while he is playing well, he isn’t playing as well as a healthy Thomas is capable of.

Peter Smyth asks: I’m wondering about the “punch” play that Washington used to get Skattebo to fumble in OT and used on Likely’s second TD (didn’t count as a fumble). I guess I’ve never noticed a defensive player just standing there and making no attempt at a tackle, just waiting, watching the ball, then punching it as the guy goes down. 

My questions: How to protect against this play? Are the Giants doing this to other teams? Has this been going on for years and I’m just noticing it? Isn’t this on the head coach to prevent? It must work a lot if they are trying it. Interested in your thoughts. 

Ed says: Peter, I am not crazy about the play. It is legal, though, and has been around for a while. It does seem to be becoming more of a thing in recent years. Yes, the Giants do it to other teams. Jevon Holland is good at it. I have seen Arvell Reese try to do it. It is becoming standard practice when one defender has a player under control for the next defender to try and punh the ball out. Tell me what a head coach is supposed to do about it. If a runner has the ball securely in two hands with a good grip on it and a defender punches the ball in the right spot with enough force it is going to come out.

Maybe the smartest thing a runner can do is realize when it’s time to stop fighting for six more inches and get to the ground before somebody knocks the ball out.

Bob Donnelly asks: With Sunday’s tie the NY Giants are in first place in the NFC East and, with a .700 winning percentage (3.5 /5), have the third best record in the NFC. Could you please share the scenarios of how, at the conclusion of the 18 game season, a tie helps/hurts a team?

Ed says: Bob, tie games count as a half-win and half-loss. So, let’s say the Giants and Eagles both finish with nine wins atop the NFC East. The Eagles, unless they also tie a game this season, would be 9-8. The Giants would be 9-7-1. The way the NFL looks at ties, they would technically be 9.5-7.5, so they would have the better record and would be division champs.

This played out in 2022. The Giants were 9-7-1. They made the playoffs as a wildcard. The 9-8 Detroit Lions went home without a playoff berth. Right now, there is no way to know what all of the scenarios will look like at the end of the year.

ctscan123 asks: Hey Ed, I do not understand any resistance whatsoever to J.J. McCarthy being a Giant. I don’t see how it could be considered anything less than a slam dunk. It’s a fifth-round pick for a quarterback drafted 10th overall who missed his entire rookie season due to injury and started only 10 games in his second year. The expectation that young quarterbacks should make the leap from college to the NFL and immediately hit the ground running is bordering on ridiculous. If he develops into a starting quarterback, whether for us or for another team after we’ve developed him, it’s an absolute steal in terms of trade value. If he becomes a competent backup, it’s still a good deal. And for those keeping track, regardless of whether he blossoms and supplants Winston, we do actually need a backup quarterback this year. If he fails, you’ve lost a fifth-round pick. For Pete sake, what is the hit rate on fifth round picks in the NFL? I’m not much of a gambler, but isn’t this deal basically all upside? What am I missing here? I know this is a rant disguised as a question which is one of your favorite things, but the opposition to this move is one of the bigger head-scratchers I’ve encountered in a long time.

Ed says: CT, where are you reading about resistance to the McCarthy trade? I have not seen much resistance to the trade itself, but everyone is entitled to his or her own feelings about whether or not the Giants should have done it. I wasn’t crazy about giving up a fifth-round pick, but the Giants felt he was the best quarterback available at the time and that the price was reasonable.

There are people who will argue the Giants simply should have signed Jimmy Garoppolo or grabbed Joe Milton off the Dallas practice squad. So be it.

There is more disagreement about when, or if, McCarthy should play.

In the end, no matter what move gets made someone always disagrees. It’s the way of the world.

The Cam Skattebo section

Jim Jordan asks: I know Skattebo is very popular in the locker room, but watching the body language of his teammates after his fumble yesterday, I have to wonder if Harbaugh needs to sit him down for a week or two and activate Singletary instead. Given how much Harbaugh talks about accountability and meritocracy, I would think it sends a pretty bad message to turn a blind eye to the fact that his starting back has now fumbled on roughly 5% of his carries this year so far. Particularly when his reaction to them luckily avoiding a loss was to say he was happy to take the tie and get out of town. What do you think? Should Harbaugh try to get Skatt’s attention with a week on the inactive list.

Gary Siems asks: Harbaugh has stressed that everyone has to earn playing time. Tracy seems to have been benched based on two preseason mistakes (missed blocking assignment and a fumble) and regular season fumble where he was using proper technique. Does Skattebo now get benched having now fumbled four times in five games? I would prefer Tracy getting more reps based on his pass catching ability and change of pace capability as a runner. Your thoughts?

Ed says: Jim and Gary, first I’m going to talk about Cam Skattebo’s reaction. What was wrong with it? If you read or watched what he said, he knew he screwed up. He said so. He took accountability. He was also simply saying he was relieved that his screwup did not lead to a loss. That’s the same reaction most Giants fans had.

Yes, Skattebo’s teammates were upset in the moment. They knew how costly the play was. If you think the head coach is turning a blind eye to the situation, I don’t think you have been paying attention.

A week on the inactive list? That’s Draconian, and in my view doesn’t help the team. I can see the distribution of carries changing somewhat, but more in an effort to spark the running game that to punish Skattebo.

Would I be shocked if someone other than Skattebo starts the game on Sunday? No. But, removing him completely is something I don’t think will happen.

Here is something Harbaugh said on Friday:

Adam Jacobs asks: Hi Ed. It is a few hours after the stress inducing but very entertaining game. The one thing I am curious about, and maybe you can enlighten me, is this. Skattebo took his gloves off (I think in OT), which can be linked directly with his OT fumble. Is there a protocol in place for gloves, or cleats, or any equipment, being used or removed during a game, especially in a quagmire such as the game was? It seems to me the last thing you want to do is remove any equipment that could help you either run on the field better or hold on to the ball better. You would think someone with a fumbling problem would wear everything possible to make sure he doesn’t drop the ball, especially when they are in position to win the game.

Ed says: Adam, Skattebo did take his gloves off late in the game. He gave a full explanation of that decision on Thursday. It came down to the conditions making it such that he felt the gloves were not helpful.

Bill Virginia asks: The Giants have a stable of running backs. They also have a fullback, which not many teams have. Unfortunately the running game is mediocre at best. It’s hard to say if its the line or the back.
Furthermore I think they need to have the fullback more involved in offense. 

My question is their best back seems to be missing. What has happened to Singletary? I believe he is the best back on the team.

Ed says: Bill, where did this idea come from that Devin Singletary is the Giants’ best running back? He has NEVER been the Giants’ best running back.

Singletary became a Giant in 2024. Tyrone Tracy took his job after four games and had 839 rushing yards with 4.4 yards per carry average to 439 and a 3.9 yards per carry average for Singletary.

In 2025, Singletary was the clear RB3 behind Tracy and Skattebo. After Skattebo was injured, Singletary became No. 2. He was still third on the team in rushing yards behind Tracy (740) and Dart (487), and averaged just 3.7 yards per carry.

Singletary has clearly declined since the first five years of his career, when his lowest yards per carry average was 4.2. He is not the answer to the Giants’ issues running the ball.

More diversity in how they run the ball to get teams to stop crowding the line of scrimmage, and perhaps more opportunities for Tracy are the best options the Giants have right now.

As for fullback, Patrick Ricard has played more snaps (116) than any other fullback in the NFL. That’s 44.96%. Only Kyle Juszczk of the San Francisco 49ers (47.68%) has played a higher percentage of offensive snaps. So, “they need to use the fullback more” doesn’t hold water.

Through five games, Ricard has the lowest Pro Football Focus run-blocking grade of his career. So, it would seem he needs to play better. Also, as Chris pointed out earlier this weekthe Giants need to be less predictablewhen Ricard is in the game.

Ed Helinski asks: In your opinion, are NFL defenders becoming so focused on punching, raking out and chopping the ball loose that they’re compromising tackling fundamentals? And how often do the Giants focus on these takeaway drills?

Ed says: Ed, tackling fundamentals? I’m not sure I’ve seen a lot of solid tackling fundamentals in the NFL for about 20 years. I think once in a while a player gets so focused on the takeaway attempt that he misses the tackle. The counter to that is the NFL is now all about those game-changing takeaways, or big plays. You have to have them to win. I couldn’t tell you what drills the Giants do. Once training camp ends, we don’t see practice. I know defenders practice a variety of drills geared toward emphasizing takeaways in the spring and summer, and I have to believe those are standard parts of practice during the season, as well.

Kölnerbigblue asks: Ed, this may sound silly but given our last 3 games on wet fields, how do kickers prepare for difficulties planting their feet on such surfaces? Do teams spray down the practice fields to simulate such ugly surfaces?

Ed says: Kolner, it’s not really something that can be practiced. Unless you happen to be practicing outdoors on a rainy day. Spray down the fields? Seriously? And increase the risk of getting multi-million dollar investments injured? Not happening.

The biggest real adjustment would come in equipment. All players, not just kickers, have access to a variety of cleat styles based on surfaces and conditions. The players have to figure out, with help from the equipment staff, what works best in whatever conditions they are playing in.

Michael Buscemi asks: Just finished watching the Washington tie I think at one point Scat was averaging 1 and 1/2 yds a carry if we’re going to be a running offense we need some lightning we can’t keep having scatterbo with 20 carries for 60 yd are thereabouts The trading deadline is November 10th do you think that the Giants might try to get some running back with some speed to help our offense.

Ed says: Michael, I think the Giants will continue to investigate all avenues to improve the roster. That will be especially true if the NFC East continues to be such a jumble, and the Giants get to the trade deadline sensing an opportunity to win the division.

That said, I keep reminding people that the Giants have to mindful that winning nine or 10 games this year and making the playoffs is not the end game. The end game is trying to be a championship contender with Jaxson Dart at quarterback, and you don’t want to give away draft resources for a short-term fix that might just help you in 2026.

That said, somebody like Tony Pollard of the 0-5 Tennessee Titans, who has averaged 4.5 yards per carry for his career and is a good pass catcher, would help the Giants. He is, 29, though, and on an expiring contract, so the price would need to be minimal.

Nicholas Carratura asks: When Dart got injured, there was some talk he could come back for the playoffs. I’ve heard some people say he’s done no matter what. I’m having trouble finding a definitive yes or no on that since most people still think the giants don’t have a chance to make the playoffs. Curious if you have info on that or an opinion on if he should even try to come back either way.

Ed says: Nicholas, you are having trouble finding a definitive yes or no because there isn’t one. The ACL was not torn, but there was damage to the meniscus, MCL, and PCL. The absolute best-case scenario is four months, which would make January possible.

An orthpedic surgeon I consulted with said that if the PCL had to be reconstructed there is no chance Dart could meet a four-month timeline. Other than being told surgery was successful we have not been given any information. So, there really isn’t an answer.

Brian Misdom asks: Hi Ed, with the run game not being nearly as effective since Dart was injured, why haven’t we seen more of Tracy? While Harbaugh has preached a meritocracy, it seems the gaffes from Skat haven’t put him in the doghouse the same way Tracy’s have (and they were primarily in the preseason).  Do you think we will see more burn for Tracy moving forward? 

Ed says: Brian, Tyrone Tracy’s snaps have ticked up the past couple of weeks. Against the Commanders, he played a season-high 17 on offense.

This follows a familiar pattern for Tracy. In 2024, he didn’t get a real opportunity until Week 5 when Devin Singletary got hurt. Last season, he was an afterthought until Skattebo got hurt halfway through the season. Both years, he put up good numbers.

There is a certain way John Harbaugh wants to play, and Skattebo and Najee Harris fit the vision more than Tracy. Yet, the results haven’t been what the Giants want and they know some adjustments will have to be made. We’ll see if one of those is more carries for Tracy, and a somewhat more varied rushing attack.

Submit a question

Have a Giants-related question? E-mail it to bigblueview@gmail.com and it might be featured in our weekly mailbag.

item.title: 5 Questions with Bleeding Green Nation
item.description: The Panthers are actually hurting less and are better rested than their opponents. Does that mean an easy victory? Here's what one Eagles writer thinks.
item.content:encoded:
The Panthers are back and they’re facing what’s left of the shockingly 2-3 Eagles as they return from a game in London just six days ago now. Tomorrow we’ll see if they are awake and healthy enough to contend with a Panthers squad that should be freshly rested from their early bye week.

To see what other storylines and shenanigans we should be on the lookout for this week, I spoke with Brandon Lee Gowton of Bleeding Green Nation to get the inside scoop on the Eagles quarterback, running back, wide receiver, and edge injuries, among other concerns. It really does sound like only one team is going to walk into this game on two feet and that may surprisingly be the Carolina Panthers. Here’s what Brandon had to say.

With Jalen Hurts out for the game, what’s next for the Eagles at quarterback?

Tanner McKee will start against the Panthers. It’s been a pretty weird run for him dating back to Week 18 of last season.

Prior to that regular season finale, there was optimism about McKee’s outlook. He had previously shined in preseason settings; so much so that the Eagles decided to rest him after their first preseason game last year.

With the Eagles deciding to rest starters in Week 18, McKee got the start and there was hope that he might be able to beat the Washington Commanders. He looked good early on in the game before DeVonta Smith left … but then much less so afterwards.

It seems like this performance shook the team’s confidence in him because they went out and acquired Andy Dalton from your Carolina Panthers. (Great deal by Dan Morgan.) It was originally thought that Dalton was only being brought in to be QB3 behind Jalen Hurts and McKee … but in OTAs it became apparent that there was a real QB2 battle going on.

With neither candidate making a strong case over the other, that battle continued into the lead up of the Eagles’ Week 1 game. Dalton was Hurts’ backup for the first three weeks before his sole passing attempt with the team was intercepted in the end zone during the Eagles’ Week 3 loss.

The Eagles then demoted Dalton to QB3 before cutting him. And that’s how we got to McKee becoming No. 2 again.

It’s hard to predict how much time Hurts is going to miss due to his blood clot. McKee figures to be the starter until Hurts is back, if he even returns this season. Though it would seem like the Eagles could pivot to intriguing rookie Cole Payton at some point if they get knocked out of the playoff picture. Then again, the NFC East is looking so bad that the Eagles might hang around longer than expected.

As for what Panthers fans can expect from McKee, I’m really not sure. He looked the worst I’ve ever seen him play during offseason practices and preseaosn games. He’s also going to be operating behind the Eagles’ patch-work offensive line while missing some key skill players. I can’t say I’m very confident that he’s going to play well. But I don’t want to write him off entirely until we see him in some regular season action because he has shown signs of promise in the past.

UPDATE! As I was answering this question, the Eagles reportedly signed Dallas Cowboys practice squad quarterback Joe Milton to their roster. Guessing he’s the emergency third quarterback this week behind McKee and Payton?

Your running back position looks about as injured as the Panthers’ [insert position here]. With the signing of training camp/practice squad running back Ja’Quinden Jackson, what do you expect the Eagles ground attack to look like on Sunday?

Funny enough, they didn’t even sign Jackson (despite reporting that suggested otherwise after hosting him on a visit)! Not as of me typing this sentence, at least. They added Ian Wheeler to the practice squad instead.

But, yeah, the Eagles are really thin at running back. It looks like their top three options are going to be out: 1) Saquon Barkley, 2) Tank Bigsby (on injured reserve, and 3) Will Shipley.

That leaves the team with Dameon Pierce and Carson Steele, who were both called up from the practice squad last week. They also have Jaydon Blue and the aforementioned Wheeler on the practice squad now.

The Eagles managed to gain just 22 yards on 18 carries in Week 5. Give the Jags’ run defense, which has been stingy this season (fewest yards per carry allowed), for being stout. But it’s hard to expect the Eagles to be awesome on the ground when their offensive line is dealing with a lot of key absences and they’re down to RB4 and RB5.

I’m expecting the ground game to look a little better against the Panthers because … how much worse could it get than Week 5? That was the fewest rushing yards the Eagles have had in a game since Week 2 of the 2015 season. But there’s no good reason to expect it to fully click until we actually see it happen. Perhaps Panthers fans feel differently since Carolina is allowing the most yards per carry in the league.

Speaking of injuries, the Panthers early season has so far been defined by them. Where are the Eagles hurting the most right now, besides running back, and how will that affect their game?

The Eagles have 24 players listed on their injury report this week. Not ideal!

Here are the key positions to monitor (outside of running back):

WIDE RECEIVER — It sounds like DeVonta Smith might be able to play after being upgraded to limited in Thursday’s practice. But with Dontayvion Wicks being downgraded to not practicing, the Eagles might be without another starter as they’re getting their top target back.

OFFENSIVE LINE — Lane Johnson retired and the Eagles traded Cam Jurgens, who was struggling anyway. The Eagles opened Landon Dickerson’s practice window to return from IR but they don’t seem to be in a rush to activate him. Drew Kendall, who was brought in from the bench to play center after Dickerson got hurt and they moved Jurgens to left guard, returned to practice on Thursday in a limited capacity. If he’s healthy, he’ll probably start at center. If not, look for Jake Majors — who made his NFL regular debut last week after being called up from the practice squad — to get the nod instead. Starting right guard Tyler Steen is banged up but it seems like he might be play. The Eagles’ projected starting offensive line for Sunday: LT Jordan Mailata (pretty good starter), LG Willie Lampkin (fan-favorite undersized blocker who struggled in pass pro making his first regular season start last week), C Jake Majors (fringe roster player), RG Tyler Steen (cromulent starter now playing at less than 100%), and RT Markel Bell (massive player who is playing like a third-round rookie, which he is).

EDGE RUSHER — Starter Jalyx Hunt is out. He leads the Eagles in quarterback hits so far this season. The Eagles’ pass rush has already been lacking, so, missing him isn’t great. The Eagles are hoping Jonathan Greenard, who was limited in practice on Wednesday and Thursday, can return from an ankle injury. Rotational rusher A.J. Epenesa could also miss this week’s game. Arnold Ebiketie is also on the injury report, albeit as a full participant. The only Eagles edge rusher NOT on the injury report this week is Nolan Smith.

There are loud rumbles from columnists and fans alike that the Eagles should consider “punting” on the still young 2026 season. What’s been wrong so far and might the Eagles be eyeing the wounded Panthers as a get-right game?

I think a win here would be a pretty nice feeling for an Eagles team that’s endured a lot of chaos through the first six weeks of the season. Especially after nearly having the Los Angeles Rams beat in Week 4 and the Jacksonville Jaguars beat in Week 5.

But I struggle to give this team the benefit of the doubt. While they’re not far off from being 4-1, they would be one of the worst 4-1 teams in league history. If you look at how they rank by offensive and defensive EPA per play, they’re keeping company with winless teams in the NFL like the Tennessee Titans (whom the Eagles narrowly beat) and the Miami Dolphins.

The offense flat out sucks. It’s terrible. The offensive line is a big problem. First-time play-caller Sean Mannion hasn’t done much to inspire confidence, though it’s hard to truly get a read on him give the Eagles’ personnel turmoil. Nick Sirianni doesn’t seem to have answers to help right the ship on offense. And now Hurts is out for … who knows how long.

The defense hasn’t lived up to lofty expectations of being one of the better units in the league. That said, they have been coming on lately. There’s hope for that unit, especially if Jalen Carter continues to be more like the player we saw in Week 5. Seems like he’s getting healthier.

All told, it just doesn’t feel like it’s the Eagles’ year. And that’s OK! They’ve made the playoffs every season since 2021. They went to two Super Bowls and won one … seven years after previously winning their first-ever Vince Lombardi Trophy. They’re allowed to have a down season. The hope is that they can use this opportunity to prioritize contending in future years as opposed to doubling down on what seems to be like a lost year in 2026.

Not everyone agrees with that mindset and, well, I get it. It’s not fun to wave the white flag on the current season after looking forward to it all offseason long. But it could be what’s best for the team in the long run.

There is a lot at stake for both teams, both narratively and in the standings in this conference game. What is your final score prediction?

The Eagles are 3.5-point underdogs this weekend. They are 0-6 in six games as underdogs during the Nick Sirianni era.

The Eagles are also trying to become the first team to ever win while coming off an international trip against an opponent coming off their bye. Teams in those conditions are 0-4 so far.

Earlier this week, I had a feeling the Eagles might pull off an upset … only to then lose to the Cowboys in Week 7.

But I’m having a hard time giving the Birds the benefit of the doubt right now. Maybe the Eagles can get it going against this Panthers defense. But Bryce Young is playing well and I think he could have some success, though I largely trust the Eagles’ defense to put forth a good effort.

I’ll go with: Eagles 21, Panthers 26.

Earlier this week, we published our latest SB Nation Reacts survey, sponsored by the folks at FanDuel Sportsbook, and asked Detroit Lions fans two questions:

  1. Which Lions player returning from injury will have the biggest immediate impact? (weekly question)
  2. Are you confident the Lions are headed in the right direction? (recurring poll)

Our weekly confidence polls have been a roller coaster ride throughout 2026. After entering the season on a high note, things dipped after they needed overtime to beat the Saints in Week 1, then fell below 50% for the first time in the Dan Campbell era after a bad Week 2 loss in Buffalo. After a Week 3 win over the Jets, confidence rebounded to nearly 80%, only to plummet to 12% the following week after a loss in Carolina.

Now, after their third victory of the season, this time over the Cardinals, fans’ confidence in the team has rebounded again, though not quite to where it was before. Let’s take a look at the results of this week’s polls:

As for our second question, there was a clear winner, as anticipated, but we wanted to give readers a chance to also comment and share their view on the potential impact of two key players returning from injury. But before we get to that, let’s take a look at the results from this survey:

Let’s take a closer look at the comment section of our original article and The Feed post to see fans’ explanations for why they voted the way they did (lightly edited for clarity).

Most approved/interacted with “right direction” comments:

  • No Username: “Since a “yes” answer implies full confidence, I’ll stay with “no” until I see some consistency in the defense, and steady performance against better teams.“
  • Matt48912: “I answered “no” because I am not confident right now, but I still think they might be. I need more than 3 quarters against a team struggling more than them on defense before I think they are getting back to where they were 2 years ago.”
  • icd8u2: “Once we acquire another good CB, then I will be fairly confident we are headed in the right direction. No matter what you think of Arnold, losing your first-round CB pick for nothing in return really hurt our CB room.”
  • rbelieve: “I hope they’re headed in the right direction. But I am not “confident”.
  • critical perspective: “I keep reminding myself that there isn’t a team out there who is firing on all cylinders in every aspect of their roster. […] The Lions have an elite offense and a much improved defensive front. The LBs and, to a great extent, defensive backs have struggled, and there just may not be a fix at corner for this season. But overall, there is so much talent on this team that you’d hope they can plug some holes and keep it rolling to at least be in the conversation come January.”

He can play center field, he can play in the box as a LB, he can play the nickel. He should be what they want Clark to be, but he doesn’t have the range for anymore. Rookie Caleb Downs could be used in a different way on Sunday against the Green Bay Packers than he has been over the last few weeks. Mike Pettine is the new senior defensive assistant for the Dallas Cowboys, and the hope is that his experience brings some hope to a struggling unit.

Cowboys could have new plan for rookie Caleb Downs ahead of Sunday’s showdown vs. Packers – Joseph Hoyt, Dallas Morning News

The Cowboys have adjusted how they’ve used Caleb Downs over the last few games due to players being banged up. However, a change back to his original usage could be coming.

FRISCO — The Cowboys have used rookie first-round pick Caleb Downs mostly at safety over the last two games due to injuries in the team’s secondary.

“That’s not the design for Caleb,” Cowboys coach Brian Schottenheimer said this week. “We want Caleb down near the line of scrimmage.”

That could be the design against the Packers on Sunday

Pettine ready to lend support, experience to Cowboys’ defense – Todd Archer, ESPN

Mike Pettine is now in Dallas after he planned on being away from the league for a while. His mission is to give everything he’s got for his close friend Christian Parker as a senior defensive assistant.

The subject of joining the staff was first broached in the winter, but Pettine had recently announced his retirement. Pettine visited the Cowboys in the spring and was with the coaches for a few days.

Pettine will be in the coaches booth during games while Parker will remain on the sideline.

“I’m just obviously trying to hit the ground running here,” Pettine said. “I feel like I’m trying to sip water from a firehose but trying to get caught up on all the film and make observations here and there. Blake Grupe has kicked for two NFL teams, but never for a legitimate contender.

That changes Sunday when Grupe plays his first game for the struggling but still-plenty-of-upside Rams.

The 2-3 Rams, who opened the season as Super Bowl favorites, released kicker Harrison Mevis after last Monday’s overtime loss to the Buffalo Bills and signed Grupe from the New York Jets practice squad.

“I know I’m showing up to a very good team that’s on a mission this year,” said Grupe, who has played for the New Orleans Saints and Indianapolis Colts. “And I’m just hoping to do my part to push it along.”

Read more:Sean McVay backs Rams' special teams coach, hopes new kicker will rejuvenate unit

All of the Rams’ losses — to the San Francisco 49ers, Denver Broncos and the Bills featured special teams miscues.

In the 37-34 defeat by the Bills, Mevis missed a 50-yard field-goal attempt, and a potential winning 48-yard attempt in overtime that was blocked.

Grupe said he watched the game.

“We’re all in this together,” Grupe said of kickers. “Nobody wants to be in that position. I’ve been in that position.”

Grupe, a fourth-year pro, has made 86 of 105 field-goal attempts. He played nearly three seasons for the New Orleans Saints before he was released in late November 2025. He signed with the Indianapolis Colts and made all 11 of his field-goal attempts.

“Those five weeks in Indy were seriously big for me, big for my career,” Grupe said. “I was able to get the ball rolling and show what I can do.”

Grupe kicked in windy conditions at the Rams’ Woodland Hills facility on Thursday and Friday.

“I do feel confident based on what I’ve seen, and then his experience to put him out there and go execute at a high level,” coach Sean McVay said.

item.title: Sean McVay knows Rams must quickly fix special teams problems. 'Let's have solutions'
item.description: Rams coach Sean McVay is eager to see improvement on special teams this week against the Cardinals after mistakes played a role in a loss to the Bills.
item.content:encoded:
Though not part of an NFL punter’s official job description, Ethan Evans was on the phone seeking information again this week.

Evans called players who were holders for new Rams kicker Blake Grupe in New Orleans and Indianapolis.

“I was like, ‘Hey, what do I need to know about him?’” Evans said. “‘Is there anything special he wants with holds?’”

Evans is accustomed to the research.

In 2023, the Rams replaced Brett Maher during the season with Lucas Havrisik, and then eventually re-signed Maher. Last season, Harrison Mevis replaced Joshua Karty at midseason, and now Grupe replaces Mevis.

Read more:Sean McVay backs Rams' special teams coach, hopes new kicker will rejuvenate unit

Special teams miscues — including surrendering a 70-yard kickoff return, a missed field-goal attempt and a blocked field-goal attempt — helped doom the Rams again Monday in a 37-34 overtime defeat by the Buffalo Bills at SoFi Stadium.

On Sunday, the struggling 2-3 Rams will attempt to bounce back against the struggling Arizona Cardinals (1-4).

“I want to see this get fixed,” coach Sean McVay said of special teams breakdowns, adding, “Let’s have solves, let’s have solutions and let’s give our players a chance to be able to have 11-as-one executed in each phase as consistently as possible.

“That’s what we’re going to keep striving for,” he said before quipping, “and I’m hopeful that it does happen so I don’t have to keep talking about it.”

Said special teams coordinator Bubba Ventrone: “It ultimately comes down to reverting back to your fundamentals and your techniques that enable you to be able to protect, block, tackle, all of those things.”

Read more:Rams vs. Arizona Cardinals: How to watch, start time, score prediction and odds

After playing four of their first five games against teams that made the playoffs last season, the Rams will face a Cardinals team coached by former Rams offensive coordinator Mike LaFleur.

LaFleur is the latest former Rams offensive assistant to be hired as a head coach. His older brother Matt LaFleur coaches the Green Bay Packers, Zac Taylor the Cincinnati Bengals, Kevin O’Connell the Minnesota Vikings and Liam Coen the Jacksonville Jaguars.

Former Rams defensive coordinators Brandon Staley and Raheem Morris also parlayed their time under McVay into head coach roles.

“As much as I love Sean, haven’t really thought of him too much,” Mike LaFleur told Arizona reporters this week, “and I’m sure he’s kind of feeling the same way about me right now.”

McVay said he talks with LaFleur “a lot.” But had not this week, “just because it’s been busier than normal, but I will talk to him at some point.”

Read more:NFL Week 6 picks: Panthers defeat Eagles; Packers beat Cowboys

McVay was busy releasing Mevis and signing Grupe, and dealing with the NFL’s suspension of left tackle Alaric Jackson.

The league initially suspended Jackson for two games for striking Bills linebacker Bradley Chubb in the face on the field after the Rams’ defeat. The suspension was reduced to one game on appeal.

Veteran David Quessenberry, a ninth-year pro who last started a game in 2023, will start in place of Jackson as quarterback Matthew Stafford’s blindside protector.

“This is kind of why I’m here — when things like this happen,” Quessenberry said. “So I’m ready to go. This is what I’ve worked for ... I’m fired up.”

item.title: Explosive plays haunt Maryland’s defense amid four-game skid
item.description: The Terps have allowed 34 plays of 15 or more yards through six games.
item.content:encoded:
Maryland football had more momentum than it could’ve hoped for away to No. 5 Ohio State on Saturday. The Terps had just flipped a Buckeyes fumble into three points, shrinking their deficit to 7-3 late in the first quarter.

It was all gone two plays later.

After running back Ja’Kobi Jackson powered for three yards, quarterback Julian Sayin faked the handoff and quickly connected with tight end Nate Roberts over the middle. The sophomore, who had blown past linebacker Carlton Smith, sprinted untouched for a 68-yard touchdown. 

Those lapses have become a regular occurrence for Maryland’s defense, which has allowed three consecutive opponents to post at least 40 points. While head coach Mike Locksley has stressed the need to limit explosive plays, his faltering secondary continues to leave receivers open.

The Terps have surrendered 34 chunk plays — characterized as gains of at least 15 yards — this season, with Ohio State totaling seven for 243 yards. Four of the Buckeyes’ chunk plays went for touchdowns, leading to Maryland’s 45-16 defeat. 

“I think the limiting of the explosives, which to me, when they’re the passing variety like they were today, that usually comes with leverage, eye control,” Locksley said postgame.

The problem started well before the Terps’ four-game skid. Maryland allowed UConn quarterback Kalieb Osbourne to throw for 36 and 39-yard touchdowns to wide receivers JD Willoughby and Shamar Porter, respectively. Amari Jackson and Jamare Glasker, the Terps’ starting defensive backs, failed to keep pace in coverage.

While those touchdowns were not costly, Virginia Tech torched Maryland for a season-high eight chunk plays the following week. Those explosive gains were largely due to tackling issues; the Terps missed 23 tackles — their most in the last year.

Maryland allowed 445 total yards of offense, with quarterback Ethan Grunkemeyer completing 31-of-39 passes for 314 yards and three touchdowns. But most of that damage was preventable.

At the 9:24 mark in the second quarter, Grunkemeyer checked it down to running back Jeffrey Overton Jr. out of the backfield for a routine pass. Daniel Wingate quickly converged on Overton, but his diving tackle effort came up short. Three more Terps defenders had chances to bring down the running back and also missed, resulting in a 49-yard touchdown.

“We got to make a play. We had some guys in position, but didn’t come up or didn’t make the play,” Locksley said postgame. “We got to do a better job, obviously. All of us, whether it’s the tackling, whether it’s us getting off blocks, a lot of those things showed up.”

UCLA and Nebraska combined for 13 chunk plays against Maryland — amounting to 450 yards, an average of 34.6 yards per play — to help hand Maryland a combined 76-point margin of defeat. Bruins wide receiver Aidan Mizell erupted for an 83-yard receiving touchdown, with 74 coming after the catch.

While the Terps’ previous opponents found success through the air, UCLA’s rush attack ran rampant. The Bruins exploded for 266 yards on the ground.

Wayne Knight, the Big Ten’s leader in rushing yards per game and touchdowns, amassed 100 yards on just 10 carries. His 45-yard rushing touchdown was one of UCLA’s four touchdowns on the ground: Anthony Woods and Jaivian Thomas punched in short-yardage scores, while Troy Leigber added a 63-yard touchdown late.

The run defense struggles have furthered in Maryland’s last two Big Ten games, as Nebraska and Ohio State have each collected over 200 rushing yards. Cornhuskers quarterback Anthony Colandrea, while not the fastest runner, scampered for a 51-yard gain in the fourth quarter of their game. 

“Just doing our job. Being in the right position, having everybody rally to the ball, and just getting on the ground,” Wingate said of the improvements needed after the Ohio State game. “We had a lot of guys just out of position, and if you’re out of position, a team like Ohio State is going to capitalize on that.”

Ohio State wide receiver Jeremiah Smith’s first two receptions went for 33 and 40-yard touchdowns, exposing Maryland’s man coverage. Eighty-nine of his 93 total yards came after the catch.

“When we play man is where we got in trouble today, and we’ve got to be able to get the ball on the ground once it’s caught because they were catching runs and not the deep variety,” Locksley said Saturday.

The Terps have allowed a Big Ten-worst 32.7 points per game. Their inability to get players on the ground have plagued a reeling defense, with 718 yards after the catch conceded and 85 missed tackles this season.

Maryland will need to erase those gaping secondary holes Saturday against Rutgers in a must-win game for both teams.

item.title: Prospects of interest for the Bengals in the Ohio State vs. Indiana game
item.description: Talent galore in a top-10 showdown in Bloomington
item.content:encoded:
With the Bengals on a bye week this week, and Ohio State traveling to face the defending National Champion Indiana Hoosiers, it feels like a good time to sneak a little draft talk into the mix. There are a ton of talented skill position players in this game, including Heisman favorite Jeremiah Smith.

However, the Bengals are not going to be in the market for a first round wide receiver. Even if they were, they are not going to be in a position to take Smith. Charlie Becker and Nick Marsh are ultra-talented receiver prospects for the Hoosiers, but enough about the skill players.

Austin Siereveld

Siereveld has played all over the line for the Buckeyes the last few seasons. He has experience playing everywhere but center for Ohio State. Ultimately, his best position may be at guard at the next level. The Bengals Dalton Risner is playing good football, but is scheduled to be a free agent after the season.

The Bengals drafted Brian Parker II in the sixth round, and he will have an opportunity to be a future starter somewhere on the Bengals line. When you want to compete for Super Bowls, you will need depth on the offensive line regardless. A player like Siereveld with his versatility should be of interest to every team in the league.

Amare Ferrell

Jordan Battle is coming off a really solid performance against Miami. However, that doesn’t take away from some of his early-season struggles in the secondary this season. Battle still misses too many tackles and is scheduled to be a free agent after the season. The Bengals could decide to bring in another day two safety to fill his spot.

Amare Ferrell is an experienced safety prospect for the Hoosiers, having already eclipsed 2,000 snaps during his career. He has good enough size for the position at 6’2” and 205 pounds. He possesses impressive ball skills with 8 interceptions over the previous two seasons. Ferrell is a player to keep an eye on at safety. The Buckeyes have a couple of players at the position that could be mid-round draft selections also. Those guys are Earl Little Jr. and Jaylen McClain.

Jermaine Mathews

Mathews is another experienced defensive back. He has played over 1,600 career snaps earlier at corner. He has the flexibility to play in the slot or on the outside. He currently has a 76.0 coverage grade during the 2026 season. He played pretty well going up against the Texas Longhorns’ talented receivers during week two. This week will be another big test for Mathews against Becker and Marsh.

Mathews doesn’t have the greatest size at around 5’11” and 195 pounds, but he is a physical player. Mathews is a more than willing tackler, instinctive in zone coverage, and should test fairly well at the combine this year. The Bengals will have a decision to make at corner with both DJ Turner and Dax Hill scheduled to hit free agency after the season. Even if they bring both of those guys back, you can never have too much depth at the corner position.

I would expect an early-round investment at the position come April.

item.title: Panthers' JJ Jansen to play his 282nd game, most ever for a long snapper
item.description: Carolina's JJ Jansen will become the NFL's all-time record holder for games played by a long snapper on Sunday.
item.content:encoded:
Carolina's JJ Jansen will become the NFL's all-time record holder for games played by a long snapper on Sunday.

The Panthers-Eagles game will be Jansen's 282nd, breaking a tie with Trey Junkin for the most games played at long snapper in NFL history.

The 40-year-old Jansen long snapped at Notre Dame and then signed with the Packers as an undrafted free agent in 2008 but played only in the preseason, spending the regular season on injured reserve. In 2009 the Panthers needed a long snapper, so they traded a conditional 2011 draft pick for Jansen. He's been their long snapper ever since.

Long snapping is a skill that few players ever learn, and most who do have a story of a football mentor who taught them the technique that can earn playing time on the varsity high school team, a college scholarship for some, and NFL riches for a select few. For Jansen, that mentor was his father, who had been a high school long snapper.

"I still remember we practiced in the same way every single time," Jansen told Darin Gantt of Panthers.com. "We had like a square piece of grass that was probably 20 yards by 20 yards. I'd stand at one end in front of a tree that was right in the middle. My dad would stand at 15 yards away, and I would snap it. We'd have those legendary long nights where you're good, and then you stink, and then you're good, and you stink, and you're mad at yourself because you stink, so you yell at your dad, and he's yelling back at you and, there's this whole, you know, boys and their fathers moments."

Jansen has played the second-most games of any active player, behind only Ravens defensive end Calais Campbell, who has played 283 games. If both Campbell and Jansen play all 17 games this season, at the end of the year Campbell will have played 295 games, tying him with Darrell Green for the 16th-most in NFL history, and Jansen will have played 294, good for 18th-most in NFL history.

All 281 of Jansen's games have been with the Panthers. Former Lions kicker Jason Hanson has the NFL record for most games played with one team, at 327. If Jansen keeps playing every game in Carolina, he'll move ahead of Hanson in the final game of the 2028 season. Jansen is showing no signs of slowing down.

Beginning with a home matchup with the 1-4 New Orleans Saints on Sunday, the Giants’ next four games are against teams with a combined 5-14-1 record. That the Giants are having success while having so much room to improve is a positive considering the strength of the coaching staff. But the margin for error has been impossibly small. The common refrain after close wins has been that the team would have lost similar games in recent seasons. It’s impossible to argue that point. Having an edge in those tight games is the reason Harbaugh’s hiring was celebrated as a franchise-altering move.

They still play strong, opportunistic defense and they can run the ball. QB Jameis Winston sure does have a bunch of good weapons to throw to as well, at least when he’s throwing to the right team.
