item.title: The cracks in the Seahawks offense last season are now chasms under Brian Fleury
item.description: The Seahawks offense is non-functioning this year. It’s a continuation of how they ended 2025.
item.content:encoded:
The Seattle Seahawks offense stinks. Ignore the points scored, which do not accurately reflect the underlying statistics, the Seahawks offense is bad. It may cost them a playoff berth, and it’s pretty much already cost them the NFC West title barring some humongous San Francisco 49ers collapse.

Seattle sits at 3-3 after a brutal 17-14 overtime loss to the Denver Broncos. The Seahawks’ three losses are by a combined eight points, but the turnover margin in those games is a combined -7. That’s not going to get it done. Sam Darnold has played poorly enough to justify talks about benching him. The running game is both banged up and an absolute mess. If not for Jaxon Smith-Njigba, the Seahawks would look like an offense befitting of their 1990s throwbacks, because Seattle’s offenses for much of the early 1990s were an impossible watch.

New offensive coordinator Brian Fleury is taking a lot of heat for the way this unit has cratered coming off a Super Bowl season. I’m not going to excuse Fleury whatsoever for this atrocious offensive slide, but I think there’s something bigger at play that stems from the tail-end of last season under Klint Kubiak.

The warning signs for the Seahawks offense were there last year

For those of you who are new to Field Gulls and/or don’t remember, I wrote a big article right before the season finale against the San Francisco 49ers. Seattle had won six consecutive games but the high-flying, high-scoring offense from the first half of the season noticeably dipped during the win streak. I’m not going to just quote myself in huge blocks and make this article a lot longer than it needs to be, so here are the CliffNotes (MookNotes?) of what I observed at the time:

  • The passing game clearly declined in efficiency from the Los Angeles Rams loss onward. The run game improved, which was a relief, but Sam Darnold’s hot start noticeably cooled and it was more than just the four-interception disaster against LA. His sack rate would’ve been worse if you took the Rams game out, actually. They were also a much more explosive offense pre-Rams loss.
  • Teams started blitzing Sam Darnold more and stacking the box less. Four of Darnold’s six highest blitz rates faced were from Week 11 onward, most notably the onslaught from Brian Flores’ Minnesota Vikings. Even the Carolina Panthers blitzed on over half of Darnold’s dropbacks. Darnold was one of the most blitzed QBs at the time (and generally performed well), but teams were sending extra heat more often. In terms of stacked boxes (8+ defenders in the box), the Seahawks went from facing stacked boxes north of 35 percent of the time to barely 30. Opposing teams stopped fretting about the running game and wanted Sam Darnold to beat them.
  • Sam Darnold’s weaknesses were exposed in pure dropback situations. When Sam was slinging it, the Seahawks were the best play-action passing team in the NFL. Put him in a spot without the play-action and things get a whole lot worse. At the time of last year’s article, Darnold was 23rd in EPA/dropback on non-PA throws, with most of his interceptions coming in those scenarios.
  • Seattle scored a lot of points by living off short fields. The Seahawks still scored at a healthy clip in part because they were getting defensive and special teams touchdowns, as well as really short fields that the offense couldn’t screw up. They led the NFL in touchdown drives starting at midfield or better from Week 12 onward. From Weeks 1-11, the Seahawks scored touchdowns on about 25% of their drives when starting inside their own 30. They scored touchdowns about 10% of the time from Week 11 onward, which ranked 28th.
  • The running game showed signs of improvement. The rushing EPA was markedly better while the success rate was only moderately better. Seattle’s passing game dropped considerably but the rushing attack found some juice as the season progressed. A great sign for how they ended up performing in the Super Bowl.

My buddy Griff (cmikesspinmove on Twitter and BlueSky, one half of the Seattle Overload podcast), provided some more perspective on how flat the passing offense in particular was after Darnold’s torrid start.

Things have only gotten worse for the Seahawks in 2026

  • The Seahawks offense is not good at virtually anything right now even though Jaxon Smith-Njigba is having a dominant season. They rank 25th in EPA/play, 18th in EPA/pass (almost certainly propped up by Drew Lock’s showing against the Arizona Cardinals), 31st in EPA/rush, 9th in sack rate, 16th in net yards/attempt, 28th in third-down conversion rate, 18th in red zone touchdown rate, and 16th in yards per play.
  • Sam Darnold is playing like a bad quarterback in play-action or dropback. Darnold is 24th in EPA/play on play-action passes, heavily hampered by his three interceptions and no touchdown passes, and 25th in EPA/dropback on non-PA throws, right behind Bo Nix. So nothing is working for Darnold and his turnovers are absolute game-sinkers.
  • Defenses are stacking the box even less than last year and Seattle can’t take advantage. While fully acknowledging the Jadarian Price and Zach Charbonnet injuries, Seattle cannot run the ball explosively. The stacked box rate is 23.6%, 15th in the NFL and nine percentage points lower than 2025. The Seahawks rank 25th in EPA/rush against light boxes, and their yards after contact against light boxes is 19th after being 11th in 2025. Over the past two games, the Seahawks faced stack boxes at a 15% clip, and the Seahawks running backs put up zero explosive runs against the San Francisco 49ers and three against the Broncos.
  • Yes, Sam Darnold is still getting blitzed a lot, and he’s the literal worst QB when pressured. Darnold has been blitzed on almost 37% of his dropbacks, fifth-highest rate in the NFL. Last year is was 34.8%, so it was already high and now it’s even higher. When he’s pressured, he is essentially a non-functioning quarterback. This is his EPA/dropback. Dead last.

Keep in mind that Darnold was 30th in this same stat last year, so this is a two-year trend of the same problem. When he’s under duress he is at his worst, and the offensive scheme and pass protection only exacerbates his chronic weakness.

  • The Seahawks still cannot consistently score touchdowns without reasonably good field position. Seattle has now had 40 drives at or inside of its own 30-yard line this season. Only five of those have turned into touchdowns, which ranks 26th (via Stathead). Their touchdown drives during this ugly three-game stretch have traveled 23, 65, 20, 68, 24, 23, and 67 yards. They’re average TD drive length from Week 4 onward is 41 yards. When Drew Lock started against the Cardinals, they did have 86-, 80-, and 70-yard touchdown drives, while Darnold had 90- and 80-yard TD possessions against the Washington Commanders. That’s it. But the pattern from late last year has bled into this year: Seattle’s offense is stuck when it isn’t starting possessions effectively a couple of first downs away from field goal range. You cannot live like that.
  • The running game is horrendous. I’ve already given some stats earlier in this section, but when Kenneth Walker III and Zach Charbonnet (up until his injury) caught fire it saved the offense. That’s not happening with Emanuel Wilson and George Holani. So if the passing game structure is broken and there is no running game as a fallback option, you are screwed.
  • We have to be honest with how much Klint Kubiak protected this offensive line. Hawkblogger had this great question and stat about Seattle’s max protect usage. Last year they were first, this year (prior to last night) they were 27th. That means a lot more responsibility belonging to the offensive line than previously delegated.

This offensive line is not performing well and I do not think Fleury is helping with his play-calling. Maybe the most dispiriting thing for Seattle outside of Darnold’s drop in form is that this o-line may not be as good as hoped. Not all of this falls on Darnold when seasoned veterans like Abe Lucas are getting put in the spin cycle by Nik Bonitto, or the interior is getting overwhelmed by superior defensive tackles.

It’s easy and simplistic to just go, “Run what Kubiak ran last year!” and that’s how you change the offense. But Klint isn’t here anymore, and there were clear signs that Kubiak’s offense had hit certain walls before finding a crevice to victory through the rushing attack. If nothing else, Kubiak knew what concepts Sam liked and executed well, and those two put together a masterclass in the NFC Championship. I’m not sure if the same applies for Fleury.

There’s a cynical part of me that believes Kubiak maxed out what he could to make Sam a well-functioning quarterback, and that there really isn’t a way forward with Sam as a starter because of his long-standing weak spots in pure dropback situations. With non-elite quarterbacks there are only so many levers you can pull before competent defenses respond. Another part of me believes Brian Fleury’s offense is not helping Darnold (or, really, even his offensive line) nearly enough to be put in more optimal positions to succeed and look more like the QB we saw in 2024 and 2025.

Either way, dating back to the homestretch of last year, we’re almost the equivalent of a full season of the passing offense not being particularly sharp outside of JSN, and opposing defenses have largely figured out how to turn the play-action money machine off and now they have no reason to respect the run until further notice. Blitz Darnold, pressure Darnold, and you can even live with JSN feasting if it means nothing else of note gets accomplished. Seattle needs answers fast, or else this season is going to be a bust and cause a significant rethink of this offense heading into next offseason.

item.title: NFL Network analyst has doubts about Eagles’ Jalen Hurts story
item.description: NFL Network analyst Michael Robinson thinks there's more to the story behind Jalen Hurts’ injury.
item.content:encoded:
NFL Network analyst Michael Robinson thinks there’s more to the story behind Jalen Hurts’ injury.

During an appearance on “NFL Gameday Kickoff” on Thursday, Robinson, a former Pro Bowl fullback, theorized that the Eagles could be using Hurts’ injury as a means to eventually move on from the quarterback.

“They’re incentivized to go into the draft and maybe look for a quarterback,” Robinson said, mentioning Philadelphia’s slew of 2027-28 draft picks acquired in recent trades.

Despite Hurts’ stellar seven-year tenure with the Eagles, he hasn’t performed well to start the season under new offensive coordinator Sean Mannion, and with his contract ending after the 2028 campaign, Robinson speculated that Philadelphia could be planning to move on from the three-time Pro Bowl QB.

“It looked like they were trying to pin the outcome of this season on Jalen Hurts just so that they could have an excuse later on to move on from Jalen Hurts,” Robinson continued. “And, again, I’m not saying I know nothing, guys. But if I’m just playing devil’s advocate here, and I’m thinking that way, if I’m Jalen Hurts — or anybody in Jalen Hurts’ camp — I’m saying, ‘Well if everybody’s hurt, I’m hurt, too.’

“To me, it looked like Jalen is kind of getting himself out of the fray so that this lost season … he’s pulling himself out so that this doesn’t look like it’s on me.”

Hurts, 28, was sidelined this week while dealing with a superficial blood clot in his calf. Philadelphia was aware of the injury since it was suffered during the Eagles’ 24-20 loss to the Rams on Oct. 4.

The Eagles have yet to provide a timetable on Hurts’ return, and no one around the organization has indicated anything suspect surrounding the QB’s injury.

Medical experts said that the blood clot could sideline Hurts for at least 45 days, depending on the course of treatment going forward.

“A lot of times, what we’re doing is kind of following people closely over time,” Dr. Jordan Schaefer, a hematologist at the University of Michigan Health System and associate professor of internal medicine at the University of Michigan Medical School, told USA Today Sports of potential treatment options.

“It’s not like a one-time visit and then you’re done. It’s often reassessment in how you’re feeling and a physical of how the leg looks. Is that swelling and redness and exam getting better?”

The Eagles are likely to start Tanner McKee in Hurts’ absence, while rookie Cole Payton should slot into the No. 2 role. However, Philadelphia reportedly signed Joe Milton off the Cowboys’ practice squad on Friday, adding another signal-caller to the room.

item.title: NFL predictions: Bears will bounce back big against the Falcons

item.content:encoded:
I know some Chicago Bears fans are down after that loss to the Green Bay Packers, but was Week 1 really that long ago? Are we letting the game in the pouring rain and three straight starts by backup quarterbacks cloud our outlook for the Bears? After an offseason of real hope, hype, and anticipation, Caleb Williams and the Chicago offense dropped 59 points in a road game to kick off the year. Sure, the defense was exposed a bit, but the Bears were the talk of the NFL.

After that Week 1 performance, the offseason buzz around Williams as a dark-horse Most Valuable Player candidate ramped up even more, as a bunch of money poured in on him to win MVP, thus lowering the odds.

Then a tough battle against an aggressive Minnesota Vikings defense came in a downpour, and Williams was carted off. Most thought the season was doomed, but the injury wasn’t season-ending, and the Bears regrouped to go 2-1 in Caleb’s absence.

Week 6 for the Bears is a road game against the Atlanta Falcons, and our partners at FanDuel Sportsbook currently have the Bears at -1.5, with the over/under at 51.5.

A road favorite with some uncertainty at quarterback is exactly what the Bears were one week ago, and we all remember how that one turned out.

But this time, the talk is positive about Caleb starting for the first time since Week 2. He practiced on Thursday, said he could do everything, had another practice today, and was full again, presumably with no setbacks.

Assuming he plays*, I like the Bears to win and cover the 1.5 points. I also like the over on the total because Atlanta’s offense will get theirs.

I also like the over on Williams’ passing yards, set at 225.5 by FanDuel.

There’s still plenty of season left, so if you think Caleb can get his MVP case back on track, those odds are at +10,000. Not gonna lie, a few bucks on that at those odds could be a fun one to monitor.

*If the Williams doesn’t play, I still like the Bears to win and cover, but I’d stay away from the total.

item.title: Rams ‘Conductor’ finally meets his match — and gets a surprise he’ll never forget
item.description: Rams defensive tackle Kobie Turner, known for his signature sack celebration, got a surprise visit and custom gift from LA Opera's music director.
item.content:encoded:
Los Angeles Rams defensive end Kobie Turner has spent the better part of his four NFL seasons conducting chaos in opposing backfields. On Friday afternoon, the Los Angeles Rams defensive tackle finally got a lesson from someone who actually knows how to wield the baton. 

And this maestro didn’t need to sack a quarterback to earn his title.

Following Rams practice, Turner received a surprise visit from Domingo Hindoyan, the new music director of LA Opera, who arrived wearing a Rams jersey and bearing a gift fit for the man affectionately known as “The Conductor.”

Hindoyan presented Turner with a custom conductor’s baton inside an engraved case featuring his name, nickname and No. 91. He even offered the Rams star a few pointers on conducting an orchestra.

For Turner, whose signature sack celebration features him waving an imaginary baton, the moment struck a different chord.

“It’s really cool to be able to represent that we’re more than just athletes,” Turner exclusively told The California Post. “It took me back to when I was multitasking and playing football in college, and then going right after classes to take my conducting classes.”

Turner isn’t some football player pretending to be a musician for social media clicks. The former University of Richmond double major in music and mathematics has performed in a cappella group, played piano, released singles and dazzled fans with his powerful singing voice.

His renditions of “House of the Rising Sun” and Chris Stapleton’s “Tennessee Whiskey” have showcased a talent that extends well beyond the gridiron. In 2024, Turner competed in Season 12 of the Masked Singer on FOX as “Goo.” He was eliminated in the quarterfinals of the show.

His ultimate dream after football? Becoming a choir director.

“I’m living my dreams,” Turner said. “I’m playing the game that I’ve always wanted to play. I have a wife, I have a kid, and I’m still able to live that life while continuing to keep music a part of it.”

Hindoyan, who will conduct Georges Bizet’s Carmen at LA Opera from Oct. 17 through Nov. 7, invited Turner and his family to attend the production in downtown Los Angeles. The opera stars Rihab Chaieb and Joshua Guerrero.

Members of LA Opera also got a taste of Turner’s day job, participating in football drills and hitting blocking pads during their visit.

Naturally, that raised one important question: Could Turner return the favor and conduct the orchestra?

“That would be crazy. That would be a whole lot of work,” Turner laughed. “Maybe I could conduct four bars or something, but that’s his world.”

As for the engraved baton, Turner plans to find a special place to display it at his offseason home in the Virginia area where he and his wife grew up. 

“It looks awesome,” he said of the baton. “I might have to send it back to my house and figure out how to get a really nice display for it.”

item.title: Isaiah Likely emerging as Giants star after years in Mark Andrews’ shadow
item.description: Isaiah Likely is proving his worth with the Giants, ranking second among NFL tight ends with 33 catches after leaving Mark Andrews' shadow.
item.content:encoded:
John Harbaugh pours over hundreds of hours of college football tape every spring — more than most NFL head coaches — but Isaiah Likely’s highlights at Coastal Carolina stick in his brain.

Get texts from Paul Schwartz with all the latest Giants news and insights, exclusive to Sports+ subscribers.

tRY IT NOW

“When he was being evaluated — he went in the late fourth round — nobody really could get their arms around him,” Harbaugh said. “He made all these plays in college, but it just looked different. In college, he also was crazy good as a perimeter blocker. He would launch guys through the air — like 5 yards through the air sometimes.” 

Harbaugh and Likely are first-year Giants but fifth-year partners after four with the Ravens, where Likely was stuck behind Pro Bowler Mark Andrews on the depth chart. 

The Ravens made their choice between them by re-signing Andrews to a three-year, $39.3 million extension last December — all but guaranteeing Likely’s free agent departure (three years, $40 million). 

“Knowing that when teams focaled [Andrews] in as the guy, how did he attack every day differently?” Likely said. “Because it’s easier when your team is scheming you up wide-open looks, but when the defense is actually honing you in and knowing that, ‘We have to stop that guy, how do you take the next step to be in that type of schematic?’ And that was something that Mark taught me, whether it was watching film or at practice. And now I feel like once I got it, I was good with it.” 

So far, so good, indeed. 

With Harbaugh’s inside knowledge, were the Giants right in thinking that Likely was an elite tight end in hiding? Likely’s 33 catches rank No. 2 in the NFL among tight ends and are only nine shy of his single-season career high. 

Five games into his tenure, Likely already is the first Giants veteran free agent addition with multiple games of two or more touchdown catches at any point in his contract since Plaxico Burress in 2005. All the other players to do so in between were acquired through the draft or undrafted rookie signings. 

“[In] college, you’re put in situations usually in a system where if you’re the guy they … try to make you win [your route] as much as possible,” Likely said. “And when you get to the league, it’s more about disguising defenses and really just watching a lot of film.” 

More credit to Andrews’ mentorship. 

“Being able to incorporate that in my game to now where I’m seeing the field like a quarterback, where I can see spot drops and where I can just feel spaces,” Likely said. “And when you have a quarterback that sees the same way as you or talks about it the same way as you, that’s when it’s just night and day.” 

Unlike teams that split their two best pass catchers on the perimeter, the Giants’ complement of Likely draws safety attention away from Malik Nabers. Likely has run a career-high 77.2 percent of his routes from the slot — only the Bengals’ Mike Gesicki is in the slot more among tight ends — where 195 of his 284 yards have come from, per NextGenStats. 

“I told Leek since the day I got here, ‘My job is to make sure no team is able to double cover you,’ ” Likely said. “And I feel like it’s insulting if I see a team that would rather double-cover Leek and leave everybody one-on-one than having everybody else get their one. If I’m doing that, that means [Nabers is] going for 100-plus [yards] every game because there’s not a corner, I feel like, in the league that could just stay with him one-on-one all day.” 

Tight ends coach Tim Kelly — a former NFL offensive coordinator — watched every play of Likely’s from the Ravens before free agency even though the head coach’s stamp of approval was already involved. 

“You saw the stuff that you are seeing now — his ability to make plays, his ability to block in space and put his face on people in the run game,” Kelly told The Post. “That’s why he’s here. He was behind a great player, but it was intriguing to think, ‘What can he do with more opportunities? His ability to catch the ball away from the framework of his body and his body control, he’s got a lot of cool traits that show up consistently whether it’s a Wednesday or a Sunday.” 

One thing that the Giants don’t like is calling him a “receiving tight end.” 

“He’s not just a receiver,” Kelly said. “Are his blocks going to look similar to Theo Johnson’s or Chris Manhertz’s or Pat Ricard’s? No, but they all have a unique skill set. It’s his attention to detail and incredible instincts.”

item.title: Why 49ers would be wise to hold Nick Bosa back one more week
item.description: Barring the unexpected, Nick Bosa's bold proclamation a week ago won’t come to fruition. That's not necessarily bad news for the 49ers.
item.content:encoded:
SANTA CLARA — It’s been a week since Nick Bosa made the bold declaration that it was “pretty darn likely” that he would be able to shake off the calf strain that’s kept him sidelined since Week 2 in time for the 49ers’ Monday night showdown against the Commanders.

And yet, still, San Francisco’s star edge rusher has been nowhere to be found.

Bosa didn’t practice Friday for the second straight day and hasn’t even been spotted off to the side during the portion open to reporters. Barring the unexpected, it would appear that his proclamation a week ago won’t come to fruition. 

Now, that might sound like bad news. And nobody would blame the 49ers Faithful, of all fan bases, to be conditioned to interpret any less-than-glowing health update in a negative light.

But let’s pump the brakes.

While Kyle Shanahan said Thursday that he was still “hoping” to have Bosa on Monday night, the 49ers coach has put his team in a position where there’s no need to force it.

Just about everything that could go right has through the first five weeks of the season. Yet another break went their way to begin Week 6, when Sam Darnold was picked off in overtime Thursday night, sending the Seahawks into the same unenviable position as the Rams:

A full three games behind the 49ers in the loss column.

San Francisco is in full control of the NFC West, but there’s been one glaring exception to its 5-0 start — all those darn injuries. Impressive as it’s been for the 49ers to stack wins while losing more bodies by the week, it’s time to cash in some of that breathing room.

Bosa is hardly the only Niner nursing nagging ailments. Mike Evans, who has toughed out broken ribs, started experiencing Achilles soreness this week. Fullback Kyle Juszczyk returned to practice but remained limited by his hyperextended knee. Defensive tackle Gracen Halton (quad), left tackle Colton McKivitz (illness) and backup guard Carver Willis (toe) were also new additions to the practice participation report.

The 49ers have given themselves the freedom to slow-play it with all of them.

Why not take advantage of it?

In theory, even if the 49ers lost both of their next two games — not ideal, nor likely — they would still go into their Week 8 bye on top of the NFC West, at 5-2. It’s not like they need Bosa to beat the Commanders or the Falcons — they sacked Darnold five times, pressured him on 40% of his dropbacks and won on the road in Seattle without their best pass rusher.

Evans is of more importance given the state of the rest of the 49ers’ receiving corps. But if there was ever a week that San Francisco could get by with Brandin Cooks and Jordan Watkins as their top two wideouts, it would be against the NFL’s 29th-ranked pass defense.

At this point, doesn’t the prospect of allowing Bosa and anybody else who needs an extra week to get fully healthy for the stretch run outweigh the cost-benefit of a win or loss? 

“We’re always toeing that line,” general manager John Lynch said Friday in his weekly appearance on the 49ers’ flagship radio network. “We want to make sure that when we get him back, we have him back for good. You know that he’s not gonna reinjure it.”

The spotlight of Monday night acts as a bit of a double-edged sword. Theoretically, the extra day would give Bosa a better chance of making it back. But on the other hand, the 49ers would have to hope and pray that his calf holds up with only six days to recover before their next game.

Shanahan said the 49ers aren’t taking the short week into account in the determination of Bosa’s chances to play this week. “It’s more about how, is he fully recovered from the calf and what are the percentages of him reinjuring that?”

But it goes without saying that the chances of reinjury go down the longer Bosa has to rest and the longer he has to recover after returning. The bye week after they play Atlanta next week presents as soft a landing as any, the best chance to set him up for a healthy second half.

In fairness, Bosa couched his confidence last week with a “possibly” and a “probably.”

But the week after, in Atlanta? “Definitely,” Bosa said.

That was the date he and the 49ers had been targeting all along.

They shouldn’t play any games with the health of arguably their most important defender.

Stick to the plan. Give him one more week. Then let him unleash the full fury of Nick Bosa.

All three were listed as limited practice participants and then designated as questionable.

Carter, who has been on a two-game heater, “looked fine” to the point that head coach John Harbaugh initially expected him to be considered a full participant. Carter’s availability is especially important given that fellow edge Brian Burns already is out for the season. 

Marcus Mbow is the swing tackle if Thomas or Eluemunor can’t play. Rookie J.C. Davis would see his first career action if both are out.

There is a breaking point where the depth chart changes, right? 

“Of course. Yes,” Harbaugh said. “There is a point.” 

Has he reached it yet? 

“We’ll see,” Harbaugh said. “We’ll find out.” 

Backups Najee Harris and Tyrone Tracy Jr. have one fumble each on limited touches this season too. Inactive veteran Devin Singletary had a fumbling issue earlier in his career. 

With Johnson out, Chris Manhertz could become the No. 2 tight end, but he mostly is a blocker. Thomas Fidone, who has appeared in one game so far, adds more as a receiver behind starter Isaiah Likely. 

“He could help us,” Harbaugh said. “He’s had great practices, runs good routes, played well on special teams last week. Thomas is ready to play, as he showed last week.” 

Hearing that WR Malik Nabers — coming off of back-to-back 100-yard games in his return from last year’s torn ACL — thinks he only is 70 or 80 percent of the way to his full capability excited Harbaugh. 

“That gets me fired up,” Harbaugh said. “I can’t wait to see the 20,30 percent more. That’s going to be fun. I mean, I think he’s doing great and he had a great week of practice, so it’s good.”

item.title: Las Vegas Raiders-Buffalo Bills FEED topic: How will offensive line respond?
item.description: The position group has been called out, but will something change?
item.content:encoded:
Heading into their Week 6 matchup against the Buffalo Bills, the 2026 version of the Las Vegas Raiders’ offensive line hasn’t looked very different than last season.

The Raiders are averaging just 3.0 yards per carry as a team and, according to Pro Football Focus, 240 of Ashton Jeanty’s 291 rushing yards (82.5%) have come after contact. Additionally, quarterback Kirk Cousins has been under pressure on 41.0% of his dropbacks in Las Vegas’ last two games, per PFF.

As a result, head coach Klint Kubiak suggested some changes to the Raiders’ trenches could be coming during his press conference on Monday after the team’s 45-17 loss to the New England Patriots.

“We have to look at everything,” Kubiak replied when asked about a potential shuffle to the offensive line, via Silver & Black Sports Network’s Jesse Merrick. “We have to improve there. It’s something I’ve been saying for multiple weeks now that’s not getting done, and so, as a coaching staff, it falls on me. It falls on me to get it fixed.” The Athletic’s Sam Warren added that Kubiak confirmed other linemen will get more opportunities moving forward.

In other words, the coach is publicly calling the position group out, and it’s up to them to respond. No one should feel like their spot is safe at this stage, leading to questions about what changes could be in store for Sunday’s game against the Bills.

Left guard Spencer Burford seems like the most logical choice to get replaced. Burford has really struggled in pass protection, giving up the most pressures (18) of any guard this season, per PFF. Additionally, his 56.6 run-blocking grade doesn’t inspire much confidence and is tied for 56th out of 81 qualifiers (minimum 85 snaps). Then again, the other guard, Jackson Powers-Johnson, has a case to get replaced, too.

Powers-Johnson has been stingier in pass protection with just nine pressures surrendered in four games. However, he’s been a problem in the running game with the fifth-worst run-blocking grade (43.8) at his position. The third-year pro has struggled with consistency throughout his career and had to fend off second-year pro Caleb Rogers during training camp to remain in the starting lineup. That sets up another potential swap.

On top of that, Kolton Miller and Tyler Linderbaum were viewed as steadying presences on Las Vegas’ offensive line heading into the campaign. However, both have left something to be desired. Miller has been charged with 12 pressures over the last two weeks, and Linderbaum’s 63.1 PFF grade for the season ranks 19th among centers.

The latter isn’t “bad” per se, but it isn’t what the organization bargained for when it made him the highest-paid interior offensive lineman in NFL history, and by a wide margin at that. Granted, it’s highly unlikely that those two are in danger of losing their respective spots at this stage. But there is certainly room for improvement.

Long story short, the only Raiders offensive lineman who has met or exceeded expectations so far this season is right tackle DJ Glaze. The 2024 third-round pick has been solid in the run game with a 62.8 mark and has made tremendous strides in pass protection, yielding just seven pressures. That gives the Silver and Black a silver lining in the trenches, but the rest of the group has some work to do and, as noted above, changes could be coming.

Rogers had a rough showing in his one start this year, filling in for an injured Powers-Johnson against the Kansas City Chiefs. But that’s a small sample size, and it isn’t like the current first-string guards are getting the job done. The Texas Tech product has exclusively played right guard under Kubiak, but he did get run on the left side during the preseason a year ago. Also, JPJ and Burford have experience playing on both sides of the line to expand the combinations that the Raiders can deploy in the trenches.

Meanwhile, rookie Trey Zuhn III was cross-trained at just about every offensive line position during training camp but has only been used as an extra lineman/jumbo tight end for 12 snaps during the regular season. He could factor into the mix at guard too, and maybe even left tackle if need be, since that was his primary college position. Granted, Zuhn missed last week’s game with a knee injury and was limited in this Wednesday’s practice.

Also waiting in the balance is second-year offensive tackle Charles Grant, whose only significant regular-season action came in last year’s Week 18 contest against the Chiefs.

So, for this week’s game day discussion on The FEED, we’ll be keeping tabs on the Raiders’ offensive line, starting with who is on the field. The game kicks off at 1:25 p.m. PST and will air on CBS (check your local listings). I look forward to talkin’ some ball with y’all!

Back in May when the NFL released the Denver Broncos 2026 schedule, I saw a brutal first six games for Denver and questioned how they could come out of that stretch above .500. In fact, my snap analysis was exactly this: “Frankly, if Denver can get through this stretch of games at or above .500 then we have to chalk that up as a major win.” Here they are at 4-2 and it feels like around Broncos County that we’re reacting to an 0-6 team right now.

We need to a little perspective. And yes, Bo Nix and the offense need to get better. They need to find a better running game. They need better interior pass protection. They need wide receivers to get better separation. Bo needs to get through his reads on scheduled. All of this has been said ad nauseum. But here’s the thing, they are 4-2 and nowhere near playing good offensive football. And 4-2 against mostly playoff contenders (ChargersLOL).

Denver has gotten through the worst part of their schedule with a winning record and have a chance to reset the whole season. Road games against the Arizona Cardinals and Carolina Panthers with a home game against the Kansas City Chiefs in between. Punch the Chiefs in the mouth and make them doubt Week 1 happened and go into the Bye Week at 7-2. This is far more possible in my mind than what they just did to get to 4-2 through the first six games.

So let’s F-in go!
